Shrine or temple? Here's the 3-second trick ⛩🛕

Look for a torii gate. If there's a torii, you're at a Shinto shrine. If you see a big incense burner, a pagoda or a Buddha statue, it's a Buddhist temple — like the Great Buddha of Kamakura in this photo.

Many places in Japan have both side by side, so it's worth looking twice.

Before you pray at a shrine, stop at the water basin first 💧

It's called the temizuya. Take the ladle with your right hand and rinse your left hand, then switch and rinse your right hand. Pour a little water into your left palm to rinse your mouth, then rinse your left hand again.

One rule people often miss: never drink straight from the ladle.

Save this for your trip 📌

📷 Hyppolyte de Saint-Rambert / CC BY 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

#Japan #JapanTravel #JapanTips #PowerSpot #JapaneseShrine #VisitJapan #TravelJapan

2 bows, 2 claps… then what? 🙏

At most shrines in Japan, the basic way to pray is:
1. Bow deeply twice
2. Clap twice
3. Put your hands together and make your wish
4. Bow once more

A few shrines have their own style (Izumo Taisha, for example, uses four claps), so follow any sign you see.

Why do locals walk on the side of the path? 🚶

At shrines, the center of the approach path is traditionally said to be the way of the kami (the gods). Many visitors walk a little to the left or right as a sign of respect, and bow lightly when passing through the torii gate.

Nobody will scold you, but it's a nice way to visit like a local.

The souvenir you can only get at shrines and temples ✍️

It's called goshuin: a hand-written ink seal that proves your visit. Bring a goshuin-cho (a small accordion-style book, often sold right there) and ask at the shrine office. It usually costs a few hundred yen.

Remember: it's a record of prayer, so visit and pray first, then ask for the seal.

Save this for your trip 📌

Drew bad luck on your omikuji? Don't worry 📜

Omikuji are paper fortunes sold at shrines and temples. If yours says bad luck, many people tie it to the special rack or rope at the shrine, leaving the bad luck behind.

Good fortune? You can keep it in your wallet as a little reminder.

Why do so many people offer a 5-yen coin? 🪙

In Japanese, 5 yen is "go-en", which sounds the same as "go-en" meaning a fortunate connection or bond. So a 5-yen coin in the offering box is a small wish for good connections — with people, luck and the place itself.

Any amount is fine, but now you know the story.

When do Kyoto's autumn leaves peak? 🍁

In a typical year, the colors in Kyoto are at their best from late November to early December. Places like Arashiyama get very busy, so go early in the morning for quieter paths and soft light.

In Kyoto this week? You're right in the season.
